title: Terminating computations for classical knot invariants

items.title: Encoded diagram size and exact output
items.statement:
Let $D$ be a nonempty finite regular oriented link diagram: a smooth immersion of a finite union of oriented circles into the plane with finitely many transverse double points, no triple points, and one overpassing branch specified at each double point. Let $c(D)$ be its number of crossings and $m(D)$ its number of components. An arc is a connected strand segment cut at each undercrossing; each component with no undercrossings contributes one closed arc. Write $a(D)$ for the number of arcs. If $q(D)$ components have no undercrossings, then $a(D)=c(D)+q(D)$ and $0\le q(D)\le m(D)$.

A supplied finite code for $D$ has code length $L$, the total number of bits in that literal code, including its tags, signs, labels, and separators. The length depends on the chosen encoding. In particular, for one of the tagged Gauss, signed Dowker–Thistlethwaite, or oriented planar-diagram formats, $L$ is the bit length of the supplied valid code in that format. The procedures in this page take typed mathematical diagrams or valid codes as stated; no string parser or malformed-code behavior is included in any operation count.

For an integer $z$, define its signed-magnitude bit length by $\ell_{\mathbb Z}(0)=1$ and $\ell_{\mathbb Z}(z)=1+\lceil\log_2(|z|+1)\rceil$ for $z\ne0$. For a Laurent polynomial $P(A)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}z_jA^j$ with finite support, define its coefficient-bit size as $0$ if $P=0$, and otherwise as $\max_{j:z_j\ne0}\ell_{\mathbb Z}(z_j)$. Its absolute Laurent degree is $\max_{j:z_j\ne0}|j|$, with value $0$ for $P=0$. For a prime $p$, elements of $\mathbb F_p$ are represented exactly by residues $0,\ldots,p-1$, and their representation uses $\lceil\log_2p\rceil$ bits.

An exact output is the complete integer, finite list, or Laurent polynomial with its integer coefficients and exponents. A floating-point approximation is not an exact output. A field-operation count treats each addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero element, and equality test in $\mathbb F_p$ as one operation; this convention does not assert that these operations have constant bit cost as $p$ varies.
items.strategy: Fix the finite input parameters and an explicit arithmetic cost model; define exact polynomial coefficient size and exact discrete output without claiming parsing or floating-point error bounds.

items.title: Dihedral Fox coloring counts are preserved by Reidemeister moves
items.statement: Let $p$ be an odd prime. A Fox $p$-coloring of a finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ assigns an element of $\mathbb F_p$ to each arc and satisfies $2x_o=x_i+x_j$ at every crossing, where $x_o$ is the overarc color and $x_i,x_j$ are the two underarc colors. If $D'$ is obtained from $D$ by planar isotopy or one oriented Reidemeister move of type R1, R2, or R3, restriction outside the move disk gives a bijection from the Fox $p$-colorings of $D$ to those of $D'$. Consequently the number of Fox $p$-colorings is unchanged along every finite sequence of such moves. The local bijections use no choice principle.
items.strategy: Prove unique extension across R1, use the involution a↦2b−a for R2, and use the right self-distributive identity for R3; inverse variants use the same involution.

items.title: Exact bracket output bit-growth bound
items.statement:
Let $D$ be a nonempty unoriented regular link diagram with $c$ crossings and $m\ge1$ components, and let $\langle D\rangle=\sum_j z_jA^j$ be its exact Kauffman bracket. Its Laurent exponents satisfy $|j|\le 3c+2m-2$, and its signed-magnitude coefficient-bit size, as defined in the encoded diagram size definition, is at most $m+2c+1$. Consequently, a knot diagram ($m=1$) has Laurent degree and coefficient-bit size bounded linearly in $c+1$.

The state-sum algorithm admits a naive exact implementation taking
$O(2^c(c+m+1)^4)$ elementary bit steps in the following model. Its typed
input gives $c$ and the number $u$ of crossingless components in
self-delimiting binary: each number is encoded by $b$ ones, a zero, and its
$b$ ordinary binary digits, with $b\ge1$ the number of those digits.
These fields are followed by the edge-pairing table on the $4c$
endpoints indexed by crossing and local port. Its entries are ordered by
endpoint index and each uses $\max(1,\lceil\log_2(4c+1)\rceil)$ bits.
At each crossing the ports are northwest, northeast,
southeast, southwest in the bracket's fixed local chart; the two smoothing
pairings are therefore fixed pairs of port indices. The table is assumed to
be the incidence data of the given diagram. Polynomial arithmetic uses dense
arrays of signed binary integer coefficients, and one tape-cell read, write,
or head move on a fixed finite number of binary work tapes costs one step.
For knots this bound is $O(2^c(c+1)^4)$. It is a bound for this explicit
indexed implementation, not for arbitrary black-box polynomial operations.
Constructing the indexed input from an arbitrary literal code of length $L$,
reading other labels or padding, and processing geometric coordinates are
outside this bound.
items.strategy: Bound the number of state circles by m+c, use the binomial l1 norm of each loop factor, sum over 2^c states, and bound the Laurent exponent interval.

items.title: Linking number and Fox coloring finite complexity
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram with $c$ crossings, $m\ge1$ components, and $a$ arcs as defined in the encoded diagram size definition. For a two-component diagram, after one constant-size component-count check, the linking-number scan visits exactly the $c$ crossings, makes at most $c$ component/sign tests and $c$ integer additions, and returns the exact integer half-sum of mixed crossing signs; its absolute value is at most $c/2$ and it is invariant under ambient isotopy of the oriented link.

For any such diagram and any odd prime $p$, the Fox coloring system has one row per crossing and one column per arc over $\mathbb F_p$. Matrix construction uses at most $2c$ field additions to combine repeated arc coefficients and $ca$ zero-entry writes. If row reduction uses $r$ pivots and has $f=a-r$ free variables, then $r\le\min(c,a)$, pivot search uses at most $ca$ entry tests, and row reduction uses at most $ra+2r(c-1)a$ field arithmetic operations. The algorithm returns exactly $p^f$ Fox colorings. Listing the full solution set after reduction uses at most $p^f(2f(a-f)+a)$ field arithmetic and output-write operations. If only the count is required, $p^f$ can instead be computed by repeated squaring using at most $2\lceil\log_2(f+1)\rceil$ integer multiplications, with at most $f\lceil\log_2p\rceil+1$ magnitude bits. The input convention gives $a\le c+m$, so these bounds depend only on crossings, components, and field size. The coloring count is invariant under ambient isotopy of the oriented link. Field operations count as unit-cost operations; no bit-time bound for those operations or polynomial-time evaluation claim is made.
items.strategy: Count crossing visits for linking number; for Fox colorings count matrix initialization, pivot searches, normalized pivot rows, elimination entries, and the separately stated output enumeration. Carry ACω only into the ambient-link-invariant clauses.

items.title: Bracket state-sum exponential bound
items.statement:
Let $D$ be a nonempty oriented link diagram with $c$ crossings and $m\ge1$ components. The state-sum portion of the normalized bracket computation visits exactly $2^c$ smoothing states; computing the writhe correction requires one pass over the $c$ crossing signs. Its exact normalized output $f_D(A)=(-A^3)^{-\operatorname{wr}(D)}\langle D\rangle$ has absolute Laurent degree at most $6c+2m-2$ and signed coefficient-bit size at most $m+2c+1$. For a knot diagram, these output bounds are linear in $c+1$.

Using the indexed endpoint-pairing input and dense signed binary-array
implementation of the exact bracket bit-growth theorem, together with the
$c$ crossing signs supplied as bits, the normalized bracket can be computed in
$O(2^c(c+m+1)^4)$ elementary bit steps. This is
$O(2^c(c+1)^4)$ for knots. Input records are assumed to describe the given
typed diagram; arbitrary literal-code reading and parsing, extra padding or
labels, and geometric-coordinate processing are outside this implementation
bound. The finite computations are choice-free. Under the Axiom of Countable
Choice, $f_D$ is an invariant of the ambient-isotopy class of the oriented
link. No polynomial-time Jones evaluation is asserted.
items.strategy: Combine the exact 2^c state count with the coefficient and degree estimates, bound |writhe| by c, and separate the choice-free diagram computation from ambient-isotopy invariance.

items.title: Enumerate Reidemeister move neighbors from a knot code
items.statement:
**Input:** A valid normalized oriented planar-diagram code $C$ for a connected one-component knot diagram, with $c$ crossings. A positive-crossing-count code records its finite crossing labels, four darts at each crossing, edge pairings, clockwise rotations, strand orientations, over/under pairs, crossing signs, and one outer face. A crossingless code records one oriented circle and its outer face.

**Output:** A finite ordered list of pairs $(E,\mu)$, where $E$ is a valid normalized one-component knot code and $\mu$ records either the finite crossing/edge relabeling identifying the unchanged planar-isotopy class or a local disk boundary, move type, and orientation/sign variant witnessing one oriented R1, R2, or R3 move from $C$ to $E$. Different labelings of the same candidate may appear more than once.

**Finite comparison rules:** Two normalized codes represent the same code class when some bijection of their finite crossing labels and edge labels carries all dart incidences, crossing rotations, orientations, signs, component cycles, and outer-face data of one code to the other. For a move-site test use the finite spherical cellulation returned by reconstruction and mark a point at infinity in its distinguished outer face. For the crossingless circle, insert one auxiliary degree-two vertex and use its two complementary face disks; this vertex is suppressed in all comparisons.

For each of $m=2,4,6$, enumerate every distribution of $m$ distinct cut points among diagram edges and every linear order of the points on each edge. Use one representative of each order (for example equally spaced interior points); their numerical positions are immaterial. In each face disk enumerate noncrossing pairings of all boundary occurrences of these cut points by interior arcs. In the distinguished face also record which complementary region contains the marked point at infinity. Glue the face arcs at the cut points and retain only choices forming a single simple closed curve. Cutting the finite cellulation along these arcs and flooding across incident cell pieces identifies the two sides; select the side not containing infinity. This is the candidate closed move disk. Its entire diagram intersection, including every vertex, edge segment and possible closed component inside it, must be isomorphic relative to its cyclically ordered boundary points to one side of a standard R1, R2 or R3 template with the chosen orientation/sign variant. In particular no additional diagram portion is permitted inside the disk. All tests are finite incidence and cyclic-order comparisons. The same construction is performed for the other code, requiring the opposite side of the same template and an isomorphism of the outside records fixing the ordered boundary points, all decorations and the infinity region. Store the cut orders, face pairings, selected regions, template variant and outside isomorphism as the certificate.

The local templates and their exact orientation/sign variants are those in the oriented Reidemeister-move definition.

**Instructions:**

1. Validate $C$ with the planar-code validation procedure. If it is invalid, return its first invalid-code result.
2. Set $N:=c+2$ and run the bounded normalized-diagram enumerator with bound $N$. It returns a finite list of reconstructed one-component knot-diagram candidates.
3. For each candidate, form the finite set of normalized code representatives obtained by assigning crossing labels and edge labels in every permitted order and applying the code's normalization rule.
4. For each representative $E$, apply the finite comparison rules. Append $E$ with a relabeling certificate if it is the same code class as $C$, or with the successful local-site certificate if a comparison certifies one R1, R2, or R3 move between them. Preserve the enumerator order and retain duplicates.
5. Return the accumulated list.

The bound $c+2$ includes every one-move result because R1 changes crossing count by one, R2 by two, and R3 by zero. This procedure lists candidates one move away; it does not decide whether two arbitrary codes are related by any number of moves.
items.strategy: Enumerate the finite arc/crossing site choices and the finite orientation/sign variants of each local move, perform the finite combinatorial code substitution, and retain exactly candidates accepted by the validator.

items.title: Breadth-first Reidemeister search
items.statement:
**Input:** Two valid normalized oriented planar-diagram codes $C_0,C_1$ for connected one-component knot diagrams.

**Output:** The algorithm returns Found(path) only if it has a finite sequence of code classes from $C_0$ to $C_1$, with a finite local-move certificate for each adjacent pair. It has no negative-output branch. It may run forever if the target code class is never reached.

**Instructions:**

1. Validate both input codes using the planar-code validation procedure. If either is invalid, return that first invalid-code result. For each valid code, form its canonical representative by checking all bijections of its finite crossing labels and edge labels, recomputing the prescribed edge normalization, and selecting the lexicographically least resulting code.
2. Set the initial frontier to the singleton containing the canonical representative of $C_0$. Initialize a discovered-code set with that representative and an empty predecessor record.
3. At the beginning of each breadth layer, test every code in the current frontier against the canonical representative of $C_1$. If one matches, follow its stored predecessor records back to $C_0$, reverse the resulting finite list, and return the path with its move certificates.
4. Otherwise, for each code $C$ in the current frontier, call the Reidemeister-neighbor algorithm. For each returned pair $(E,\mu)$, canonicalize $E$ by the finite relabeling procedure in step 1. If its canonical representative has not been discovered, add it to the next frontier and store $(C,\mu)$ as its predecessor record.
5. Replace the current frontier by the next frontier and repeat from step 3. If a layer is empty, continue with empty layers; do not return “inequivalent.”

Code equality in this procedure means equality of canonical representatives under the finite crossing/edge relabelings of the normalized code convention. Every loop in one layer is finite; the number of layers has no fixed bound.
items.strategy: Maintain finite breadth layers, canonicalize each finite code class by exhaustive relabeling, store one predecessor and move for each first-seen class, and expand every class in the current layer.

items.title: Reidemeister enumeration is only a semidecision
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $C_0,C_1$ be valid normalized oriented planar-diagram codes for connected one-component knot diagrams. The breadth-first Reidemeister search terminates with a finite move witness whenever the represented oriented knots are ambient-isotopic. If they are inequivalent, the search has no negative-output branch and does not halt with a negative answer; failure to find a path through any fixed finite depth $N$ says only that no path of length at most $N$ has yet been found. This is a semidecision result, not a decision or complexity-class result for knot equivalence.
items.strategy: Show each neighbor layer is finite and complete for one move, then induct on path length; use the oriented Reidemeister theorem for the ambient-isotopy implication and note that the algorithm has no negative branch.

items.title: A finite failed move search is not a negative certificate
items.statement: Assume ACω. For every nonnegative integer $N$ and every pair of valid normalized oriented codes for connected one-component knot diagrams, if the breadth-first Reidemeister search finds no move path of length at most $N$, then the represented oriented knot types are inequivalent.
items.strategy: Use 2N+1 explicit type-I additions for equivalence, the maximum crossing-number change of two per move for the lower bound, and the worked Fox 3-color calculation as an independent distinction of unknot and trefoil.
